steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Gaussian process-gated hierarchical mixtures of experts (GPHMEs). It should review HMEs, soft decision trees, GP-based HMEs and random-feature GPs, position our model against tree-based GP work, and summarize what GPHMEs contribute, including interpretability of deep GPs.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
HMEs and their Bayesian treatment
- novel way to build hierarchical mixture of experts (HMEs) with Gaussian processes (GPs)
- HMEs used in regression, classification, fusion; healthcare, finance, pattern recognition
- conditional mixture models; expert distributions + mixing coefficients conditioned on inputs
- maximum likelihood -> severe overfitting; Bayesian treatment via variational inference
- closest work: end-to-end differentiable amortized variational inference for HMEs, RNN approximating posterior over routing decisions

Decision trees and soft decision trees
- structural similarity: HMEs vs soft decision trees with fixed structure
- decision tree: internal nodes + terminal leaves; nodes test attributes, send sample to a child; leaves hold labels (classification) or constants (regression); single root-to-leaf path
- univariate nodes: one feature vs threshold; multivariate: linear discriminant, can be nonlinear; statistical model selection at nodes
- soft probabilistic trees: children chosen with probabilities, all paths traversed, all leaves contribute
- interpretability: Gaussian soft decision trees; DNN distilled into soft decision tree; ~ HME with experts = leaves, coefficients from gating nodes

GPs, GP-based HMEs and the GP-NN connection
- GP extensions of HMEs studied; hierarchical GP latent variable models
- GP-based HMEs mostly in function spaces, not feature spaces
- GP-NN association in several papers
- GPs ~ single-layer NNs with infinitely many hidden units -> no need to specify number of hidden units
- in feature spaces GPs help form Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) that quantify uncertainty

Sparse GPs and random Fourier features
- sparse GPs: complexity cubic -> quadratic
- three approaches: (1) inducing points, (2) Random Fourier Features (RFFs), (3) Hilbert space approximations of covariance operator (HGPs)
- RFF GPs and HGPs: no matrix decomposition, only matrix products -> faster; map inputs to linear kernel feature spaces ("feature spaces")
- we use RFF-based GPs; kernels -> activation functions: RBF ~ trigonometric, ARC-COSINE ~ ReLU
- variational learning of posterior over random Fourier features for squared exponential kernel

Related tree-based GP models
- Bayesian treed GP models: nonstationary, stationary GPs + treed partitioning
- GP-BART: Bayesian additive regression trees with GPs; standard BART has no covariance over observations -> poor performance; GP priors on each terminal node's predictions
- GP-tree: classifier for few-shot incremental learning, limited labels, works well when data scarce

Our GPHME model and DGP interpretability
- above models partition data only in input space (HMEs or soft trees); gates / inner nodes nonlinear in inputs
- GP-gated HMEs (GPHMEs): fixed complete binary trees; gating and experts use RF expansions of GPs
- decisions by GPs in linear feature spaces; much less tree complexity
- variational inference + reparameterization trick
- optimal tree height no greater than four, even with millions of samples; due to nonlinear transformation + oblique decisions
- outperforms tree-based benchmarks partitioning input data
- interpretability of deep GPs (DGPs): stacks of GP mappings, hidden layer = multivariate GP; less depth/width than DNNs; hidden layers hard to interpret; like DNN distillation into soft trees

Summary of contributions
- GPHME: novel HME using RF-based GPs
- better than state-of-the-art methods
- reduced complexity, applicable to large-scale problems
- quantifies uncertainty of GP probability distributions vs trees -> useful for decision-makers
- interpretation of DGP behaviors, explanations for leaf-node models
- extends understanding of hierarchical models; direction for future work

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In this paper we present a new approach for constructing a hierarchical mixture of experts (HMEs) using Gaussian processes (GPs). HMEs have been instrumental in many applications, including regression, classification, and fusion tasks, in different domains such as healthcare, finance, and pattern recognition. You can think of these models as conditional mixture models, where the distributions of the target variables are combinations of expert distributions. Both the expert distributions and their mixing coefficients are conditioned on the input variables. Traditionally the model parameters are estimated by maximizing the likelihood, and this often leads to severe overfitting. To address this, a full Bayesian treatment of the model based on variational inference was proposed.

Our work in this paper is closer to another line of work. There, the authors introduced an end-to-end differentiable amortized variational inference algorithm for HMEs. The algorithm uses a recurrent neural network to approximate the posterior distribution over tree node routing decisions. This makes the HME framework more flexible and efficient, and it also shows that the methods in this domain are still evolving.

Hierarchical mixtures of experts are structurally similar to soft decision trees with fixed tree structures. A decision tree is a hierarchical structure made of internal nodes and terminal leaves. In a canonical decision tree the internal nodes represent tests on attributes, and depending on the result of the test the tree sends samples to one of the children. The leaves hold the labels for classification tasks, or they are constants for regression tasks. So a sample goes along a single path from the root to one of the leaves.

The nodes of a decision tree are characterized by feature comparisons. Univariate nodes use one feature and compare it against a threshold value. Multivariate nodes define a linear discriminant in the input space for the comparisons, and this discriminant can be generalized to be nonlinear. Decision trees can also implement different statistical model selection procedures at their nodes.

Hard deterministic trees select children deterministically, but soft probabilistic decision trees select children with certain probabilities. This means all the possible paths to the leaves are traversed, and all the leaves contribute to the final decision with different probabilities.

Soft decision trees are interpretable, and this also holds for Gaussian soft decision trees for interpretable feature-based classification. In another work, a deep neural network (DNN) was used to train a soft decision tree that mimics the input-output function found by a neural network (NN). Soft decision trees give interpretability for DNNs and explainability for the representations of individual hidden layers. This is similar to a hierarchical mixture of experts with parametric probabilistic tree-based aggregation, where the leaves are the experts and the coefficients come from the gating nodes.

GP extensions to HMEs have also been studied, and hierarchical GP latent variable models have been investigated too. We see that the GP-based HME models mostly rely on function spaces and not on feature spaces.

Several papers have looked at the association between GPs and NNs. Because of the relationship between GPs and single-layered NNs with an infinite number of hidden units, GPs remove the problem of specifying the number of units in hidden layers, since they implicitly work with infinite representations. This is especially useful in feature spaces, where GP models help formulate Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) that can quantify uncertainties.

Sparse GPs are notable because they reduce the computational complexity of standard GPs from cubic to quadratic. There are three main approaches for reducing the complexity of GPs: (1) the inducing point-based approach, (2) finite basis expansion with Random Fourier Features (RFFs), and (3) Hilbert space approximations of the covariance operator (HGPs). RFF-based GPs and HGPs do not need any matrix decomposition, unlike inducing point-based methods, they only need matrix products, and this makes them faster. These two approaches transform nonlinear input spaces into linear kernel feature spaces, which we will call feature spaces from now on to distinguish them from the original input spaces.

In this paper we use RFF-based GPs. When the RFF expansion is applied to different kernels of GPs, we get different activation functions in NN. For example, trigonometric functions go with the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel, and the ARC-COSINE kernel corresponds to Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) functions. Variational learning of the posterior over the random Fourier features with the squared exponential kernel was proposed by another work.

Related tree-based GP models
- Bayesian treed GP models: nonstationary, stationary GPs + treed partitioning
- GP-BART: Bayesian additive regression trees with GPs; standard BART has no covariance over observations -> poor performance; GP priors on each terminal node's predictions
- GP-tree: classifier for few-shot incremental learning, limited labels, works well when data scarce

Our GPHME model and DGP interpretability
- above models partition data only in input space (HMEs or soft trees); gates / inner nodes nonlinear in inputs
- GP-gated HMEs (GPHMEs): fixed complete binary trees; gating and experts use RF expansions of GPs
- decisions by GPs in linear feature spaces; much less tree complexity
- variational inference + reparameterization trick
- optimal tree height no greater than four, even with millions of samples; due to nonlinear transformation + oblique decisions
- outperforms tree-based benchmarks partitioning input data
- interpretability of deep GPs (DGPs): stacks of GP mappings, hidden layer = multivariate GP; less depth/width than DNNs; hidden layers hard to interpret; like DNN distillation into soft trees

Summary of contributions
- GPHME: novel HME using RF-based GPs
- better than state-of-the-art methods
- reduced complexity, applicable to large-scale problems
- quantifies uncertainty of GP probability distributions vs trees -> useful for decision-makers
- interpretation of DGP behaviors, explanations for leaf-node models
- extends understanding of hierarchical models; direction for future work

Several papers have looked at the association between GPs and NNs. Sparse GPs are notable because they reduce the computational complexity of standard GPs from cubic to quadratic. There are three main approaches for reducing the complexity of GPs: (1) the inducing point-based approach, (2) finite basis expansion with Random Fourier Features (RFFs), and (3) Hilbert space approximations of the covariance operator (HGPs). Some recent contributions in the field that are relevant to our work are Bayesian treed GP models, GP Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (GP-BART), and GP-trees. What is different about it is that it uses GPs inside additive regression trees. In standard BART there is no covariance structure over the observations, which can lead to poor performance, and GP-BART extends BART to fix this weakness by assuming GP priors for the predictions of each terminal node. The GP-tree work presents a GP-tree-type classifier designed for few-shot incremental learning. The model deals with the challenges of learning from limited labeled examples, and it works very well when data is scarce. There is also other recent work in this space.

All the models above partition the data only in the input space, either as HMEs or as soft decision trees. That is, the gating models or the inner nodes are nonlinear functions of the inputs. In this paper we propose GP-gated HMEs (GPHMEs), which have structures of fixed complete binary trees and where both the gating and the expert models rely on RF expansions of GPs. This means decisions are made by the GPs in linear feature spaces, and the complexity of the trees is reduced a lot. We optimize the GPHMEs with variational inference and by using the reparameterization trick. The results show that in practice the optimal height of a tree is no greater than four, even for large-scale data sets with more than millions of samples. Our tree structure is smaller because of the nonlinear transformation of the input space and the oblique decision mechanisms that are created. Also, the GPHME outperforms the tree-based benchmarks that partition the input data.

Our model can also be used to give interpretability of deep GPs (DGPs). DGPs are deep belief networks built from a stack of GP mappings, where each hidden layer is a multivariate GP. In practice DGPs need less depth and width than DNNs. But with DGPs it is a problem to interpret the hidden layers. In a similar way to how DNNs are made interpretable by distilling them into soft decision trees, this paper gives ways to get insights into how a DGP makes its decisions.

To summarize, this paper introduces a GPHME model, which is a new HME that uses RF-based GPs. We also show that the GPHME is better than existing state-of-the-art methods. The proposed method also has reduced complexity and can be applied directly to large-scale problems. With our approach we can quantify the uncertainty of GP probability distributions compared to trees, and this gives useful insights for decision-makers. We also give a method for interpreting DGP behaviors and explanations for the models on the leaf nodes. Our contributions extend the current understanding of hierarchical models and give a promising direction for future research and applications.

steps.text:
In this paper, we present a novel approach to constructing a hierarchical mixture of experts (HMEs) using Gaussian processes (GPs). HMEs have been instrumental in a wide array of applications, including regression, classification, and fusion tasks across diverse domains such as healthcare, finance, and pattern recognition [1]. These models can be conceptualized as conditional mixture models, where the distributions of target variables are expressed as combinations of expert distributions. The expert distributions, along with their corresponding mixing coefficients, are conditioned on the input variables. Traditionally, model parameters are estimated by maximizing the likelihood, a practice that often leads to severe overfitting. To address this challenge, a full Bayesian treatment of the model based on variational inference was proposed in [2].

Our work in this paper aligns better with [3]. In that paper, the authors introduced an end-to-end differentiable amortized variational inference algorithm for HMEs. The algorithm incorporates a recurrent neural network to approximate the posterior distribution over tree node routing decisions. This not only enhances the flexibility and efficiency of the HME framework but also underscores the ongoing evolution of methodologies within this domain.

Hierarchical mixtures of experts are structurally similar to soft decision trees with fixed tree structures. We recall that a decision tree is a hierarchical structure composed of internal nodes and terminal leaves [4,5]. A canonical decision tree is composed of internal nodes that represent tests on attributes. Based on the results of the test, the tree assigns samples to one of the children. The leaves on the other hand hold the labels for the classification tasks or are constants for the regression tasks. As a result, a sample traverses a single path from the root to one of the leaves.

Decision tree nodes are characterized by feature comparisons. Univariate nodes use a single feature, comparing it against a threshold value [5]. In the case of multivariate nodes, they define a linear discriminant in the input space for comparisons [6,7], with the ability to generalize this discriminant to be nonlinear [8]. Decision trees can implement various statistical model selection procedures at their respective nodes [9].

In contrast to hard deterministic trees, where children are deterministically selected, soft probabilistic decision trees involve selecting children with specific probabilities [10]. This means traversing all the possible paths to the leaves, and the final decision is collectively contributed by all the leaves with varying probabilities.

The interpretability of soft decision trees extends to Gaussian soft decision trees in the context of interpretable feature-based classification [11]. In [12], a deep neural network (DNN) was used to train a soft decision tree mimicking the input-output function discovered by a neural network (NN). Soft decision trees provide interpretability for DNNs and explainability for the representations of individual hidden layers. This approach is akin to a hierarchical mixture of experts with parametric probabilistic tree-based aggregation [1], where the experts correspond to the leaves, and the coefficients are derived from the gating nodes.

GP extensions to HMEs have also been studied, [13,14], and in [15], hierarchical GP latent variable models have been investigated. We observe that the GP-based HME models rely mostly on function spaces rather than feature spaces.

The association between GPs and NNs has been addressed in several papers [16,17,18,19]. Given the relationship between GPs and single-layered NNs with an infinite number of hidden units [20], GPs alleviate the challenge of specifying the number of units in hidden layers by implicitly operating with infinite representations, This is particularly beneficial in the context of feature spaces, where GP models contribute to the formulation of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) capable of quantifying uncertainties.

Sparse GPs are notable for their ability to reduce the computational complexity of standard GPs from cubic to quadratic. Three main approaches to complexity reduction of GPs include the (1) inducing point-based approach [21], (2) finite basis expansion using Random Fourier Features (RFFs) [22], and (3) Hilbert space approximations of the covariance operator (HGPs) [23]. Unlike inducing point-based methods, RFF-based GPs and HGPs do not require any matrix decomposition, and instead, they only need matrix products, which makes them faster. These two approaches transform nonlinear input spaces into linear kernel feature spaces, hereinafter referred to as feature spaces to distinguish them from the original input spaces.

In this paper, we work with RFF-based GPs. The application of the RFF expansion to various kernels of GPs yields distinct activation functions in NN. For example, trigonometric functions are associated with the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel, while the ARC-COSINE kernel corresponds to Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) functions [24]. Variational learning of the posterior over the random Fourier features when the squared exponential kernel is used was proposed in [25].

Some recent contributions in the field and relevant to our work include Bayesian treed GP models [26], GP Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (GP-BART) [27], and GP-trees [28]. The Bayesian treed GP models allow for nonstationary modeling that couple stationary GPs with treed partitioning. The GP-BART approach from [27] introduces a Bayesian additive regression trees methodology based on GPs. This approach is distinguished by using GPs within the context of additive regression trees. Namely, in standard BART, there is no covariance structure over the observations which may lead to poor performance. The GP-BART model extends BART to address this weakness by assuming GP priors for the predictions of each terminal node. In [28], the authors present a GP-tree-type classifier specifically designed for few-shot incremental learning scenarios. The model addresses challenges in learning from limited labeled examples, and it works very well in scenarios where data is scarce. Other recent work in his space include [28].

The above models, partition the data only in the input space, either in the form of HMEs or soft decision trees. In other words, the gating models or the inner nodes are nonlinear functions of the inputs. In this paper, we propose GP-gated HMEs (GPHMEs) with structures of fixed complete binary trees where both, the gating and expert models, rely on RF expansions of GPs. This allows for making decisions by the GPs in linear feature spaces and for a considerable reduction of the complexity of the trees. We optimize the GPHMEs by using variational inference and by exploiting the reparameterization trick. The results show that in practice the optimal height of a tree is no greater than four even for large-scale data sets with more than millions of samples. The smaller size of our tree structure is a result of the nonlinear transformation of the input space and the oblique decision mechanisms that are created. Further, the GPHME outperforms the tree-based benchmarks that partition the input data.

Our model can also be used to provide interpretability of deep GPs (DGPs). DGPs are deep belief networks based on a stack of GP mappings, where each hidden layer is composed of a multivariate GP. In practice, DGPs require less depth and width compared to DNNs. However, the DGPs encounter the problem of interpreting the hidden layers. Similar to the interpretability of DNNs distilled by soft decision trees [12], this paper provides ways of getting insights into understanding how a DGP makes its decisions.

To summarize, this paper introduces a GPHME model, a novel HME that uses RF-based GPs. We also demonstrate the superiority of the GPHME over existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the proposed method has reduced complexity and is readily applicable to large-scale problems. With our approach, we are able to quantify the uncertainty of GP probability distributions compared to trees, providing valuable insights for decision-makers. Additionally, we offer a method for interpreting DGP behaviors and offer explanations for the models located on the leaf nodes. Our contributions extend the current understanding of hierarchical models, offering a promising direction for future research and applications.
